name: The old City Cemetery, graves north of North Avenue

grade.why: Known from maps or written records; no picture of it has been found.

documented_range.note: Half cleared after 1866, the rest of the graves still there in October 1871 (Colbert and Chamberlin, pp. 140, 265-266); the scene's phase begins in 1860.

change_note: Built T-3689 (2026-11-20): the refuge in the old City Cemetery, on the landmark_1871 archetype.

placement.position_note: Inside the 1871 plan's 'Old City Cemetery parcels' (data/context/1871/plan.json, from Mitchell's 1870 map), at its west side by North Clark Street, where the jaunt's families sit. The footprint's origin is local E 446.0 N 2788.0.
placement.symbolic_location: The old City Cemetery, east of North Clark Street and north of North Avenue, at the south end of Lincoln Park.

footprint.note: The patch of ground the graves are laid out in, not a lot: the cemetery runs on north and east of it (the plan's envelope).

fire.note: The fire passed over the cemetery; 'the torches alight head first upon the hollow graves', the pine head-boards burned and the dead-house with them, and the people stamped the brands out (Colbert and Chamberlin, p. 267). The stones and mounds stand; the head-boards are not modelled burning.

value.note: THE OLD CITY CEMETERY, built by T-3689 for the 1871 scene: the city's burial ground on the lake shore north of North Avenue, 'practically vacated since 1866, but all of the bodies had not been removed' (Colbert and Chamberlin, Chicago and the Great Conflagration, 1871, p. 140), taken into Lincoln Park by the act of February 1869 (p. 139). On Monday 9 October some thirty thousand people fled here from the burning North Side with what they could carry, and sat among 'some old headstones scattered about, and many, with their mounds, still standing among the thick undergrowth of grass and small oak trees' (pp. 265-266); the fire swept past, burned the pine head-boards and the dead-house, and moved on north (pp. 266-268, 287). This record is a part of the ground, round the place the jaunt stops: graves, headstones and head-boards. Every grave's place is reconstructed.

composition.note: Graves, headstones and pine head-boards as Colbert and Chamberlin describe them (pp. 265-267); their number, rows and places are reconstructed, about two graves in five left where the plots were cleared.

kind.note: Open burial ground, half cleared, where the crowd sat among the graves (Colbert and Chamberlin, pp. 265-266): the walker reads it and lets the visitor walk in it; nothing in the mesh comes from it.

wall_material.value: Grass-grown mounds, limestone and marble headstones, pine head-boards

function.note: The old City Cemetery (Colbert and Chamberlin, pp. 139-140).

built.note: In use before 1866, when it was 'practically vacated' (p. 140); when the first grave was dug here is not researched, and 1843 stands for it.

citations.citation: Elias Colbert and Everett Chamberlin, Chicago and the Great Conflagration. Cincinnati and New York: C. F. Vent; Chicago: J. S. Goodman & Co., 1871.
what_it_supplies: A citywide ratio of building materials before the fire: in spring 1868, 35,654 wooden buildings to 3,712 of brick and stone (about nine in ten wooden).
The city's 59,500 buildings in 1871 by division, with the West Division largest (29,400).
Descriptions that the West Side's burned blocks were nearly all frame, and that the South Division's burned centre held the city's most expensive structures.
what_it_does_not_supply: A material for any particular lot, block or street; a material ratio by division or for 1871 itself; paint colours.

citations.citation: S. Augustus Mitchell, Jr. Chicago. 1870. Approximately 1:31,000. University of Illinois Map and Geography Library; Wikimedia Commons surrogate.
what_it_supplies: Named streets and diagonals, river courses, lake edge, lakefront railroad and lagoon relationships, rail corridors and named parks.
Coverage from Fullerton Avenue to Thirty-first Street and Western Avenue to Lake Michigan.
what_it_does_not_supply: Individual building footprints, occupants, exact paving, engineered widths or elevations.
The western extension to Fortieth Avenue or southern continuation to Egan Avenue; these require separate evidence and reconstructed geometry.
